title: APE1 (apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1): newly identified post-translational modifications (PTMs)
projectDescription: APE1 (apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1) is a multifunctional protein essential for both DNA base excision repair and redox signaling. However, its post-translational modifications (PTMs), which are key to modulating its cellular functions, remain largely uncharacterized due to their dynamic and labile nature. In this study, we developed a novel biotin-regulated avidin-based magnetic nanoparticle platform (bMIPAPE1) that selectively captures active APE1 from living cells under native conditions. This approach preserves labile PTMs and enables downstream mass spectrometry-based proteomic analysis. Using this tool, we identified 27 previously unreported PTMs at 18 distinct residues, including modifications with critical functional implications, such as phosphorylation at Y269 and dual acetylation/palmitoylation at K228. Furthermore, we uncovered PTMs associated with subcellular localization, including modifications at K203, C208, and K63 that correlated with APE1 nuclear export. Beyond enrichment and profiling, bMIPAPE1 also inhibits the enzymatic functions of APE1 in cells, offering potential therapeutic relevance. This project showcases an innovative method for real-time PTM profiling of endogenous proteins in complex cellular environments, with implications for cancer biology and targeted drug discovery.
sampleProcessingProtocol: HeLa cells were cultured in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37°C under 5% CO₂. When cells reached 70%–80% confluency, they were either subcultured or subjected to magnetic transfection with bMIPAPE1, a biotin-regulated avidin-based nano-catcher for capturing endogenous APE1. For transfection, cells cultured in different formats (96-well, 24-well plates, or 100 mm dishes) were incubated with bMIPAPE1 (0.2 mg/mL in PBS) for 30 min on magnetic plates (MagnetoFACTOR-96, MagnetoFACTOR-24, or MagnetoPURE-Flask, Chemicell) at 37°C. After incubation, the magnetic plates were removed, and the cells were further cultured in fresh medium for an additional 30 min (MIP-Cell-1h samples) or 3.5 h (MIP-Cell-4h samples), depending on the experimental group. Afterward, cells were washed with PBS to remove unbound nanoparticles. Cells were then lysed on ice using a glass homogenizer in precooled PBS supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail. The bMIPAPE1-bound protein complexes were isolated by magnetic separation. The remaining lysate was centrifuged at 14,000×g for 15 min to separate the cytoplasmic fraction. Nuclear proteins were extracted from the pellets using RIPA lysis buffer with protease inhibitors. APE1 captured by bMIPAPE1 was eluted using elution buffer, concentrated via ultrafiltration (10 kDa cutoff), separated by 12% SDS-PAGE, and subjected to in-gel digestion. Mass spectrometry analysis was performed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid LC-MS system (Thermo Scientific). Tryptic peptides were analyzed by LC-MS/MS, and the raw data were searched against the UniProt human reference database using Mascot. The search parameters included full tryptic specificity, up to two missed cleavages, 10 ppm precursor tolerance, 0.5 Da fragment mass tolerance, and a 1% false discovery rate (FDR). Fixed modification: carbamidomethylation on Cys. Variable modifications: oxidation of Met and N-terminal acetylation. This sample preparation protocol enabled specific capture and detailed characterization of APE1 and its post-translational modifications in living cells.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw MS/MS data were processed using the Mascot search engine (Matrix Science) and searched against the UniProt human protein database (release 2017). Search parameters included tryptic digestion with up to two missed cleavages, a precursor ion mass tolerance of 10 ppm, and a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.5 Da. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was set as a fixed modification, while variable modifications included methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation. A 1% false discovery rate (FDR) was applied at the peptide level. Post-search filtering, annotation, and PTM analysis were performed using in-house Python scripts and visualized with Scaffold (version 5.0, Proteome Software).
